title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to automatically identify and evaluate specific tutor behaviors in authentic tutoring transcripts. The authors frame this as a feasibility problem: can LLMs reliably detect when a tutor provides effective praise or responds appropriately to a student’s math error, and can they grade the quality of those responses in a way that aligns with human coders?

The study analyzes 50 randomly selected transcripts from remote math tutoring sessions. The tutoring interactions involved college-student tutors working with middle school students in mathematics, and the data came from audio-recorded and transcribed online sessions. The authors test several LLMs, including GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM, using prompt-engineering strategies such as zero-shot and few-shot prompting, rationale forcing, self-consistency, and prompt chaining. The models were asked first to detect whether a target situation was present and then to evaluate whether the tutor’s move met a best-practice criterion.

Results show that the LLMs performed well on both detection and evaluation tasks, with high agreement against human annotations. The models were especially strong at identifying tutor praise and student math errors, and they also achieved good accuracy in judging whether the praise was effort-focused or whether the error response guided the student toward self-correction. The authors conclude that LLMs can support scalable assessment of real tutoring dialogue, but they also note that performance depends on prompt design and that subtle distinctions in language remain challenging.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small feasibility study using 50 transcripts with human annotations and no experimental comparison of learner outcomes. The methodology is clear and systematic, but it is primarily a validation/coding study rather than a causal evaluation of an educational intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising accuracy for scaling tutor-move assessment, but it does not demonstrate downstream effects on student learning or tutoring quality at scale. Its impact is therefore operational and suggestive rather than directly educationally transformative.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating the feasibility of using LLMs to assess tutor moves in real-life middle school math tutoring transcripts, specifically detecting effective praise and appropriate responses to student math errors.

finding.finding_summary: LLMs were highly feasible for scalable assessment of tutor moves in authentic tutoring transcripts, with high agreement against human coders. Across 50 transcripts, models achieved 94-98% accuracy for praise detection and 82-88% for math-error detection, and 83-89% accuracy for grading praise quality and 73-77% for grading error responses.
finding.measure: Accuracy against human annotations for filter and evaluation prompts on tutor move classification
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported in the paper; specific CIs vary by model and prompt
